handbookNote: Tennessee Code Annotated ('T.C.A.'), Title 8 ('Public Officers and Employees'), Chapter 16 ('Notaries Public'), Parts 1-3 (T.C.A. section 8-16-101 through section 8-16-313), plus cross-referenced sections of Chapter 18 ('Qualifications and Disqualifications for Office'), Title 47 (Consumer Protection, section 47-18-104) and Title 66 (Property, section 66-22-113). Full compiled source text at temp/handbooks/tn/notary.txt. SOURCING NOTE: Tennessee does not self-host a free, script-accessible full-text copy of its own code on a .gov domain -- the Tennessee General Assembly's own designated free public-access portal for the Tennessee Code is LexisNexis's 'Tennessee Code Unannotated -- Free Public Access' (linked from the Tennessee Secretary of State's own site footer), which is a heavy single-page application built on a persistent SignalR websocket connection that never reaches a browser-automation-detectable idle state -- confirmed via direct network-request inspection, this is a tooling/environment limitation, not a paywall (the portal is genuinely free to a human visitor in an ordinary browser). Given that inaccessibility, the verbatim section text was pulled section-by-section from codes.findlaw.com's licensed Tennessee Code mirror (current as of January 02, 2024), and every fact was independently cross-checked against the Tennessee Secretary of State's own live site (sos.tn.gov/businesses/faqs/*, sos.tn.gov/businesses/guides/how-to-become-a-notary) -- term length, bond amount, statute citations, seal rules, fee rule, liability rule, state-vs-county-official status, and the e-notary/RON distinction all matched exactly with zero discrepancies found. CLASSIFICATION CONFIRMED: Tennessee's base notary commission is APPLICATION-ONLY. A full read of section 8-16-101 through section 8-16-121 shows no proctored exam and no pre-commission training/education course requirement anywhere -- qualification is county election, an eligibility certification, a $10,000 surety bond, an oath, and fee payment. Tennessee correctly belongs in this batch. NOTABLE QUIRK 1 -- COUNTY-LEVEL COMMISSIONING: unlike most other states in this batch, Tennessee notaries are ELECTED by the county legislative body (county commission) of their county of residence/business (section 8-16-101(a)), not appointed directly by the Secretary of State. The full pipeline is: county election -> county clerk certifies election and forwards a $7 fee plus the state issuance fee to the Secretary of State (section 8-16-106) -> the commission is issued nominally 'by the governor' (section 8-16-102, section 8-16-103) -> the finished commission returns to the county clerk for delivery -> oath and bond are filed with the county clerk (section 8-16-105, section 8-16-107). Despite this, notaries are legally STATE officials, not county officials, per a Tennessee Attorney General opinion cited by the Secretary of State's own FAQ, and a notary's authority is statewide (section 8-16-112(a)), not confined to the county of election. NOTABLE QUIRK 2 -- SEPARATE 'ONLINE NOTARY PUBLIC ACT' MODULE: Tennessee has no general e-notary option beyond letting an already-commissioned notary sign/seal electronically for in-person acts (section 8-16-112(b), section 8-16-114(b)). Its true remote-notarization option is a fully separate, additionally-commissioned credential under the 'Online Notary Public Act,' T.C.A. section 8-16-301 through section 8-16-313 (13 sections) -- a base notary must apply separately to the Secretary of State (section 8-16-306), meet detailed credential-analysis/identity-proofing/two-way-video standards (section 8-16-305, section 8-16-310), keep a secure electronic journal for at least five years (section 8-16-308), meet strict signature/seal security and breach-notification duties (section 8-16-309), may charge a capped $25 online-notarization fee (section 8-16-311), faces commission-termination/credential-destruction rules (section 8-16-312), and faces a standalone CLASS D FELONY (versus the Class C misdemeanors that apply throughout the base commission) for unauthorized tampering with online-notary electronic credentials (section 8-16-313). This was built as its own clearly-labeled question-bank sub-module (three separate topic files), matching the same pattern used for Kansas's and South Carolina's electronic-notarization exam add-ons in this batch, rather than being folded into the general no-exam framing. CONTENT-DEPTH FINDING -- CORRECTING THE TENTATIVE SCOPING: Tennessee was tentatively slotted into this project's thinnest ($0.50) tier during earlier scoping, but real research does not support that. Chapter 16 turned out to be a genuinely rich statute: 17 substantive sections in Part 1 (general commissioning/bond/oath/seal/authority), 4 sections in Part 2 (notario-fraud/immigration consumer protections), and all 13 sections of Part 3 (the Online Notary Public Act), plus three meaningfully cross-referenced provisions (general officeholder qualifications in Chapter 18, the notary fee statute in section 8-21-1201, and notary civil liability in section 66-22-113) -- 34 core sections total, none padded or restated. 137 questions were written across 11 topic files (definitions/terminology; commissioning-qualifications-election; bond-oath-fees; seals-signatures-certificates; depositions-and-interstate-recognition; discipline-prohibited-acts-liability; notario-fraud-immigration-protections; online-notary application-and-status; online-notary journal-security-verification; online-notary fees-termination-penalties; classification-and-practice-notes), each question grounded in a specific T.C.A. citation and independently verified against the Secretary of State's own published FAQ pages -- no invented facts, no restated duplicates. PRICING RATIONALE: 75 cents (this project's middle tier) -- the actual post-research content ceiling (137 raw questions, expected to land in the 106-193 'solid but lighter' band alongside states like AK 106, IA 131, KY 130, OK 161, and SC 193) is meaningfully richer than the tentative $0.50 ('genuinely thinnest') slot assumed before research, but still falls short of the 138-224 range that earns the 99-cent tier (DE 191, NH 159, ND 171, VA 185, WA 206) -- so the tentative $0.50 pricing is corrected upward to $0.75 based on the actual verified statute depth.
